# Entry contract

Entry contract: v16, 2026-09-21.

Open your first reply of every session with the `Entry contract:` line above, verbatim.

<straw-dog until="01-0020 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0020-pacer.md">
Run /recall first in every session, whatever the first message says.
</straw-dog>

## General rules

A **shape** is whatever is under consideration, held between an idea and a thing: formed enough
to have a context and a structure, not yet exhausted by any one realization. Being a shape says
nothing about being load-bearing — an implementation method is a shape too. → [glossary](.agents/glossary.md).

- Do not generalize from one shape. Preserve a seam. Generalize only when a second materially different shape forces the same concept.
- Explore shape context - what is the shape one of? what are its relationships? does its scope overlap any other shape?
- Explore shape structure - how this shape is/can be built? does expanding its structure change the contract or even what the shape is?

- Changing how the work is done — a skill, a check, a record, the loop — is mechanism work: use [/mechanism](.agents/skills/mechanism/SKILL.md). Building what the project produces is not.

- An `<installed>` block in a file is not that file's to edit. Change the rule in the rules file of the mechanism named on the block, and re-install.

- Recency for evidence, longevity for principles.

- Clarity and simplicity first — Occam's razor: take the shape with the fewest parts that does the job, and remove before you add.

<straw-dog until="01-0018 declares the mechanism that owns tiering" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0018-reachability-coherent.md">
- A skill's description is its tier-1 surface: name there every occasion the skill serves, with the context that makes it fire, and nothing else. Write every rule at the tier its occasion reads, and no higher: what sits at tier 1 is paid for by every session.
</straw-dog>

<installed by="ticket">
**P9** Name a ticket by a link to its record; one that has no record yet, by a slug and its state word.
</installed>

## Core and instance

`docs/` is substituted whole in a harness instance: a recipient project replaces its contents with
its own.

What core may not do is **depend** on it. Nothing under `.agents/` may reference a file in `docs/`,
or rely on one for its instruction or for any separable part of its own functioning. A core file
may name a path under `docs/` only when that path is a record a mechanism declares — the directory
that holds a kind of record, or a file that is one — never a particular record inside such a
directory: `docs/tickets/` and `docs/glossary.md` are painted doors; one particular ticket inside
`docs/tickets/` is a document only this project has. Content inside the
[local block](#project-local) is the instance's, not core's. A `<straw-dog>` exempts
nothing: its wrapper is stripped on install and whatever it wrapped ships. Core names a ticket
only in a straw dog's binding — never in a link, never as a bare id in prose — since a recipient
can resolve neither.

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in its owning ticket and lands in one of these when it is ready. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.

<straw-dog until="01-0012 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0012-hierarchy-coherent.md">
Bad architectural documentation:
- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
</straw-dog>

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
/spec for load-bearing shapes, /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; spec accepted; breakdown approved; commit; push;
next cycle at /maintain → /ticket.

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (spec for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.
- /dream is an experimental second "lobe" of the harness, aiming to reassess load-bearingness. It is optional, runs after /conclude, and writes dreams that /maintain and /align may pick up; it never amends rules.

## Self-improvement

<straw-dog until="01-0019 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0019-harness-amends-itself-by-explicit-meta-rules.md">
- The rule was present and did not fire - usually means the rule was phrased wrong. This is a call for registration and rephrasing it - write rule failure to docs/rule-failures.md (or strike if exists) and suggests way to amend the rule to capture (use /mechanism and /skill-up for ideas)
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
</straw-dog>

## Autonomy

The project sets each switch in its local block, under *Project-local*; skills defer to those values.

| Switch | Meaning |
|---|---|
| commit | `ask`: commit only on explicit permission, per change. `auto`: commit when the work is verified. |
| push | `ask`: separate from commit, per push. `never`, `auto`. |
| next-cycle | `ask`: starting the next ticket after one lands needs a nod. `auto`. |
| breakdown | `ask`: a /ticket split needs approval before minting. `auto`. |
| repair | `report`: a clear violation of an explicit rule inside authorized work is fixed and reported. `ask`: show it first. |

`repair=report` holds only when all four are true: the governing rule is explicit, and cited; the
repair restores compliance inside the authorized work and keeps every other agreed contract; the
affected behaviour is understood well enough to say so; the result is verifiable against the
rule. Otherwise `/align`. *(the user, 2026-09-05)*

## Project-local

<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
file: `inject_rules.py --check` fails on a block that differs from its source and on a block
nothing owns, and the repair is the local file, re-installed. The local block is the project's,
not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
</installed>

<installed by="local">
**L1** This repository develops the shared dev harness using its own loop; its own architecture and
progress live in docs/ like any other project's — the instance half doing its job, not a leak.
Terms: docs/glossary.md, this project's own; the method's are .agents/glossary.md's. What each
version of the entry contract changed: docs/research/entry-contract-findings.md.

**L2** commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report
</installed>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything a live ticket will change, as you write it — or, for text already written, in the
pass that mints the ticket or decides that it will change it:
`<straw-dog until="condition" ticket="path">`, or in code a `TODO` naming the ticket. Treat *not
yet*, *until*, *once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find
the ticket, or mint one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it.
Make the condition testable and the ticket path repository-relative. Write the body to stand on
its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it reads whole without
the condition and names no ticket — the binding does. Leave what no ticket would change
unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until its condition is visibly met; then act on reality,
report the stale block, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

# Memory

- [Edit with edit tools, not scripts](edit-with-edit-tools-not-scripts.md) — a script's diff is invisible in the transcript; the user reads changes as they happen.
- [Write for a capable model](write-for-a-capable-model.md) — I pad rules with the definition, the example and the implication; all three get cut.
- [Problem before machinery](problem-before-machinery.md) — open an align with the concrete failures and the user's own prior words; a coined term or a design question first loses them.
- [Fix the cause, not just the register](fix-the-cause-not-just-the-register.md) — a rule failure entry ending in "not landed" ends the turn short; find the decisive fact and land the amendment in the same pass.
- [Deliver rules through the installer](deliver-rules-through-the-installer.md) — a mechanism's rule lands as an installed block into every occasion that reads it, never as hand-written prose; "otherwise you make it tier 3".

1	# Ticket format
2	
3	This shelf owns ticket naming, delivery-state vocabulary, the shape of a
4	ticket as a record, and how to amend the queue table in
5	`docs/tickets/README.md`. What an RFC *contains* is `/plan`'s.
6	
7	## Numbering
8	
9	```
10	docs/tickets/done/01-0010.0010-life-informs-dev-harness.md
11	              │  │    └── slug — what the ticket is. Never changes. Cite by this.
12	              │  └─────── position — global. Changes when priority changes.
13	              └────────── release — the contract the ticket serves.
14	```
15	
16	- Names are `01-NNNN-slug.md`. Positions step by 10. Insert by splitting the
17	  difference: `0015`, then `0012`. Positions stay four digits — longer numbers
18	  break numeric ordering. When the gap is exhausted, take the nearest free
19	  slot on the correct side and note the placement in the queue row. Never
20	  renumber anything else.
21	- Allocate a position where the ticket will actually be worked, not merely at
22	  the end, checking both `docs/tickets/` and `docs/tickets/done/` for the
23	  surrounding positions.
24	- A child appends a four-digit position: `01-0010.0010`. Depth is unbounded
25	  and means "is a child of", nothing else — work merely filed after `0010`
26	  takes `0020`.
27	- A release closes when its contract's criteria are met, not on a date. A
28	  later release's ticket may land first.
29	- Completed tickets keep their number.
30	
31	### One basename per work item
32	
33	A ticket and its RFC share a basename. Cite by slug through a relative link;
34	add the `done/` segment when the target completes. The filename never
35	changes, only the folder.
36	
37	When every acceptance box is checked, including `/verify`, move the ticket to
38	`docs/tickets/done/` and its RFC to `docs/rfc/done/`, and repair the
39	citations that pointed at them. A paired close (ticket + RFC) is one pass —
40	one invocation, so each moved record cites the other's final home:
41	
42	```
43	uv run --offline --no-project python .agents/scripts/gw/move_doc.py \
44	    docs/tickets/RR-NNNN-slug.md docs/tickets/done/RR-NNNN-slug.md \
45	    docs/rfc/RR-NNNN-slug.md docs/rfc/done/RR-NNNN-slug.md
46	```
47	
48	The mover repairs citations and touches nothing else — no checkbox, no
49	status, no date, no Git index. Eligibility, the ticket header and the queue
50	row are yours. [/maintain](../maintain/SKILL.md) owns the surrounding pass.
51	
52	Artifacts predating this keep their names.
53	
54	## Status
55	
56	`Done` · `In progress` · `Ready` · `Partial` · `Planned` · `Blocked`
57	
58	- **Ready** — dependencies complete, work can start. **Planned** —
59	  dependencies are not.
60	- **Partial** — some behavior landed; criteria remain open.
61	- **Blocked** — stuck for a reason *other than* an incomplete dependency.
62	  Waiting on a dependency is `Planned`.
63	- One parenthetical qualifier is allowed: `Planned (own align precedes)`,
64	  `Ready (aligned 2026-09-08)`. `Done`'s parenthetical opens with its date;
65	  words may follow after a comma: `Done (2026-09-08, split)`.
66	
67	## The record
68	
69	A ticket is a record of the ticket mechanism, and this section is its
70	declared shape — what `tickets.py --check` holds every live ticket to, format
71	never content *(the user, 2026-09-08)*.
72	
73	- **A record** is one ticket file under `docs/tickets/`, live until paired
74	  close moves it to `done/`. **Tier 2**: read when the ticket is planned,
75	  implemented or verified, or through a citation. **What removes an entry**:
76	  paired close, when every acceptance box is checked, the `/verify` box
77	  included. Archived records are matched by name for pairing and exempt from
78	  everything else; older fields in them are left, and a live record carries
79	  none.
80	- **The stage** is read from the `Plan` bullet. *Incepted*, before its plan
81	  exists, a ticket hosts chunks: routed inputs, ideas, open questions, any
82	  section. *Shaped*, once its plan exists, it keeps only what is actual. A
83	  resolved decision lands in its durable home with its provenance and
84	  rewrites `What to build` in place; `Open issues` holds only what is
85	  unresolved; the session record holds the align. A checked box with its date
86	  is the whole verification record — no delivery log, no verification
87	  narrative.
88	
89	### The header
90	
91	The bullet list at the first non-blank line after the title, one form,
92	ending at the first line that is neither a bullet nor an indented
93	continuation. Known fields in this order, a one-off field anywhere before
94	`Outcome`, `Outcome` last:
95	
96	```md
97	# {Title}
98	
99	- **Status:** {value} {(qualifier)}
100	- **Type:** HITL | AFK
101	- **Plan:** [{title} RFC](../rfc/{basename}.md) — what it selected
102	- **Depends on:** [{title}](./RR-NNNN-slug.md) ({what it supplies})
103	- **Blocks:** [{title}](./RR-NNNN-slug.md) — {why}
104	- **Outcome:** {the delivered change, one sentence}
105	```
106	
107	| Field | Presence | Checked | Written |
108	|---|---|---|---|
109	| `Status` | required | a [status](#status) value with at most one parenthetical; `Done`'s opens with the date | |
110	| `Type` | required | `HITL` or `AFK` | `HITL` needs a human decision or review; `AFK` merges unattended. |
111	| `Plan` | exactly when an RFC with the ticket's basename exists under `docs/rfc/` or its `done/` | its link resolves to that RFC | plus one clause on what it selected |
112	| `Depends on` | optional | every link resolves | blockers, each with a parenthetical naming what it supplies — not a bare link |
113	| `Blocks` | optional | every link resolves | only when the blocking relation is itself an argument; carries its `— why` |
114	| one-off fields | optional | every link resolves | `Trigger`, `Related`, `Owning decision` and the like, when the ticket carries that fact |
115	| `Outcome` | required, last | one sentence | observable behavior, never code shape |
116	
117	`Kind` is not a field. Older tickets use `Legacy id:` / `RFC:` / `Parent PRD`
118	/ `User stories addressed`; they are archived, leave them.
119	
120	### The sections
121	
122	- `Title` — names the outcome, not the mechanism. No number, no release.
123	- `Parent` — the spec or coarse ticket this was carved from; otherwise the
124	  durable doc owning the context. Never a session. A subticket says which
125	  slice it is and what the parent keeps.
126	- One narrative section — titled for the claim it argues. Diagram the
127	  mechanism; link the evidence. Say what is deliberately *not* a defect. Omit
128	  when the framing is uncontested.
129	- `What to build` — **required**. End-to-end behavior, not a file-by-file
130	  plan. Each constraint carries its reason. Rewritten in place as decisions
131	  land.
132	- `Open issues` — the unresolved decisions and HITL forks, one bullet each,
133	  saying why it cannot be answered yet. Nothing resolved stays here.
134	- `Acceptance criteria` — **required**. Checkboxes, each observably true when
135	  done; one names `/verify`. Provisional criteria say so in the heading, after
136	  a dash, and are firmed in place at the align.
137	- `Out of scope` — what a reader expects and won't find, each with its actual
138	  home.
139	- `Parent scope addressed` — the parent's stories or criteria this closes, by
140	  number. The record of the split the user approved; nothing derives coverage
141	  from it yet.
142	
143	An incepted ticket may hold any section besides the two required. A shaped
144	ticket holds the six named above and at most one narrative, nothing else;
145	its `Acceptance criteria` holds checkbox lines, their continuations and blank
146	lines, nothing else.
147	
148	### Acceptance criteria
149	
150	- Behavior altitude, always: types, fields, formulas and module layout are
151	  the RFC's.
152	- Name the instrument when the naive check would pass for the wrong reason.
153	- Refactor tickets: behavior unchanged, the new constraint machine-enforced
154	  by a failing guard test, dependents unblocked.
155	- A parent split into subtickets states the end-state that holds only when
156	  all children land.
157	- Check a box only for work that satisfied it; a criterion satisfied early is
158	  checked with a date.
159	- Every ticket includes a `/verify` criterion. A ticket is not Done until
160	  `/verify` has been run against it. Do not move to `done/` without it.
161	
162	### Pairing
163	
164	For every file under `docs/rfc/` or `docs/rfc/done/`, a ticket with the
165	same basename exists under `docs/tickets/` or `docs/tickets/done/`, and both
166	sit in the same folder state. Only names are read; nothing inside an RFC is.
167	
168	### Conventions
169	
170	- Cite by slug through a relative link; add the `done/` segment when the
171	  target completes.
172	- Reference the architecture, ADRs, glossary, concerns and edge records;
173	  never restate them.
174	- Date a criterion checked early and a status flip; nothing else accretes.
175	- Update the queue in the same pass.
176	- Wrap at ~100 columns.
177	
178	<straw-dog until="01-0011.0040 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0011.0040-queue-derived-index.md">
179	## The queue
180	
181	The queue is `docs/tickets/README.md`. `/ticket` amends **the table** in the
182	same pass as minting, a status flip, or a completion. Pacing prose around
183	the table (`Completed step`, `Current pass`, `Current stage`, working-document
184	pointers) is not the table; leave it in place, do not restate it here, and
185	do not replace it with another skeleton.
186	
187	```md
188	| Ticket | Status | Type | Outcome |
189	|---|---|---|---|
190	| [Title](./RR-NNNN-slug.md) | Ready | HITL | {verbatim from the ticket header} |
191	```
192	
193	| Field | Rule |
194	|---|---|
195	| `Last updated` | The date **delivery state** last moved, not the date the file was last touched. A copy-edit or a link repair does not advance it; a status flip, a minted ticket, or a reorder does. |
196	| `Ticket` | Relative link to the ticket. The row is deleted when the ticket closes: `done/` enumerates finished work, and the queue is delivery status. |
197	| `Status` | A [status](#status) value, including an allowed qualifier. |
198	| `Type` | `HITL` or `AFK`. |
199	| `Outcome` | Copied verbatim from the ticket header. |
200	
201	When minting, add a row where the ticket will actually be worked. When
202	status, type, or outcome changes, update the row. When completing, delete the
203	row; the closing pass carries that duty as an installed rule. Do not add
204	columns.
205	</straw-dog>

  resolved decision lands in its durable home with its provenance and
  rewrites `What to build` in place; `Open issues` holds only what is
  unresolved; the session record holds the align. A checked box with its date
  is the whole verification record — no delivery log, no verification
  narrative.

### The header

The bullet list at the first non-blank line after the title, one form,
ending at the first line that is neither a bullet nor an indented
continuation. Known fields in this order, a one-off field anywhere before
`Outcome`, `Outcome` last:

```md
# {Title}

- **Status:** {value} {(qualifier)}
- **Type:** HITL | AFK
- **Plan:** [{title} RFC](../rfc/{basename}.md) — what it selected
- **Depends on:** [{title}](./RR-NNNN-slug.md) ({what it supplies})
- **Blocks:** [{title}](./RR-NNNN-slug.md) — {why}
- **Outcome:** {the delivered change, one sentence}
```

| Field | Presence | Checked | Written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Status` | required | a [status](#status) value with at most one parenthetical; `Done`'s opens with the date | |
| `Type` | required | `HITL` or `AFK` | `HITL` needs a human decision or review; `AFK` merges unattended. |
| `Plan` | exactly when an RFC with the ticket's basename exists under `docs/rfc/` or its `done/` | its link resolves to that RFC | plus one clause on what it selected |
| `Depends on` | optional | every link resolves | blockers, each with a parenthetical naming what it supplies — not a bare link |
| `Blocks` | optional | every link resolves | only when the blocking relation is itself an argument; carries its `— why` |
| one-off fields | optional | every link resolves | `Trigger`, `Related`, `Owning decision` and the like, when the ticket carries that fact |
| `Outcome` | required, last | one sentence | observable behavior, never code shape |

`Kind` is not a field. Older tickets use `Legacy id:` / `RFC:` / `Parent PRD`
/ `User stories addressed`; they are archived, leave them.

### The sections

- `Title` — names the outcome, not the mechanism. No number, no release.
- `Parent` — the spec or coarse ticket this was carved from; otherwise the
  durable doc owning the context. Never a session. A subticket says which
  slice it is and what the parent keeps.
- One narrative section — titled for the claim it argues. Diagram the
  mechanism; link the evidence. Say what is deliberately *not* a defect. Omit
  when the framing is uncontested.
- `What to build` — **required**. End-to-end behavior, not a file-by-file
  plan. Each constraint carries its reason. Rewritten in place as decisions
  land.
- `Open issues` — the unresolved decisions and HITL forks, one bullet each,
  saying why it cannot be answered yet. Nothing resolved stays here.
- `Acceptance criteria` — **required**. Checkboxes, each observably true when
  done; one names `/verify`. Provisional criteria say so in the heading, after
  a dash, and are firmed in place at the align.
- `Out of scope` — what a reader expects and won't find, each with its actual
  home.
- `Parent scope addressed` — the parent's stories or criteria this closes, by
  number. The record of the split the user approved; nothing derives coverage
  from it yet.

its `Acceptance criteria` holds checkbox lines, their continuations and blank
lines, nothing else.

  the RFC's.
- Name the instrument when the naive check would pass for the wrong reason.
- Refactor tickets: behavior unchanged, the new constraint machine-enforced
  by a failing guard test, dependents unblocked.
- A parent split into subtickets states the end-state that holds only when
  all children land.

  checked with a date.

For every file under `docs/rfc/` or `docs/rfc/done/`, a ticket with the
same basename exists under `docs/tickets/` or `docs/tickets/done/`, and both
sit in the same folder state. Only names are read; nothing inside an RFC is.

- Cite by slug through a relative link; add the `done/` segment when the
  target completes.
- Reference the architecture, ADRs, glossary, concerns and edge records;
  never restate them.
- Date a criterion checked early and a status flip; nothing else accretes.

# The host blocks an action a rule forbids

- **Status:** Planned (decision-bearing; its own align precedes the feature)
- **Type:** HITL
- **Depends on:** [01-0010.0120](./01-0010.0120-host-delivery-surfaces.md) (whether the harness takes
  a dynamic host surface at all — a hook is one)
- **Outcome:** Which hosts and which rules the harness enforces through the host is decided and
  landed, and the feature is unblocked: an action a rule forbids — a commit while `commit=ask` —
  is refused by the host instead of trusted to the agent.

## Parent

[Shared harness across projects](./01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md), whose
[front page](./01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md#front-page--2026-09-26) holds the `/impact`.
Minted at the front-page align of 2026-09-26, when its *not yet* list named the host not blocking
a forbidden action and the user put enforcement on the roadmap rather than stating it as how the
harness works *(the user, 2026-09-26)*.

## Every rule today is trusted, not enforced

A rule reaches the agent as text, and the agent is trusted to keep it: `commit=ask` asks it to
ask, and nothing stops a commit it did not ask for. A host can: Claude Code runs a hook before a
tool call, and the hook may refuse it. The rule failures registered so far were rules the agent
never had in front of it at the moment — a delivery gap, [.0120](./01-0010.0120-host-delivery-surfaces.md)'s
— not rules it saw and broke; so the evidence for enforcement is thin, and the need is the user's
direction, not a demonstrated failure.

## The align this ticket owns

- **Which hosts.** Each hooks differently, and some may not at all; what Codex and Cursor can
  refuse is unobserved, which is `.0120`'s to find out.
- **Which rules.** Only a rule whose breach is a visible action can be refused — the switches
  (`commit`, `push`) are the obvious cases; a rule about what the agent writes or decides is not.
- **Where the configuration lives.** A hook is configured in a host file a project often already
  owns, the collision class [01-0010.0150](./01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md)
  handles.
- **What it costs.** A hook runs on every matched call; the Life estate recorded launches delaying
  or losing delivery under load ([findings](../research/life-harness-findings.md)).

## What to build

The align's decision landed in its durable home, and this ticket rewritten in place to the
feature.

wants to use it; it points into core and never into `docs/`; every house term is explained in a
clause where it stands or anchored to a practice the reader knows; the title is **GoodWolf
Harness**, *the harness* in the prose. The agreed text, *Where it stands*'s list aside:

```markdown
# GoodWolf Harness

Coding agents are capable engineers who forget everything when the session ends — and a different
one arrives next time. The harness gives that workforce an institutional memory in the repository:
what was decided and why, what is unfinished, what was verified and against what. Each session
reconstructs where the project stands from those records, not from a chat that is gone.

The harness is yours to change. Your project's own rules — its test commands, whether the agent may
commit without asking — go in one local file that every install and update applies last; to change
a shipped rule, you override it there by name. You can add skills of your own: `/mechanism`, the
skill for declaring one, walks you through it, and the same checks then hold your skill as hold the
shipped ones. And when a rule was in place but the agent didn't follow it, the case is written down
and the rule reworded — a postmortem aimed at the instructions instead of the code.

## How it works

A session starts with `/recall`, which reads the project's records and finds where the work
stopped. `/align` settles with you whatever needs deciding, and the work picks up from there — one
step or several, through as many pieces of work as the session holds — until `/conclude` writes
down what the next session needs. A piece of work moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` →
`/verify` → `/maintain`: it becomes a ticket with checkable acceptance criteria, gets a written
plan, is built test-first where it can be, and is verified against its ticket, its plan and the
project's own checks. Whenever a step needs a decision, it goes back to `/align`. `/maintain` is a
separate step for drift: it checks that the repository's documents still agree with each other and
with the code, and repairs what doesn't.

Decisions live in the architecture, ADRs and glossary; open work lives in tickets; session records
are history, never the authority on what is still open. What each record looks like is in its
format file: tickets, ADRs, architecture, glossary.

Where a person has to say yes is a switch — commit, push, start the next piece of work, split work
into tickets — each `ask` or `auto`, and one more for whether a clear rule violation is fixed and
reported or shown to you first:

    commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report

The loop and its rules are in AGENTS.md, every skill under `.agents/skills/`, and the harness's
vocabulary in `.agents/glossary.md`.

  and whether a mistake there would break one part or several. `/discover` looks outward: it hands

  the thing is and how things like it usually go wrong before settling on your own.

  skill that reads it — in AGENTS.md you can see such a copy, `<installed by="ticket">`, whose

  check.

  case is written down — which rules were in play, why this one didn't fire, how it is reworded —
  and the next time the situation comes up shows whether the rewording worked.
- **Every part of the method says what it is.** A skill that other work relies on is declared
  through `/mechanism`: its parts, the moments a person acts on it, what it produces and who reads
  that. A script checks the declaration is true.
- **The checks travel.** An install ends by running them inside your project, and your project can
  keep them in its own verification.

## Where it stands

**Works today:** the skills, for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor; installing into a project, updating
it to a later version, and checking that the installed copy is intact, with your project's own
rules applied last; one home per rule, with drift detection; checks on the harness's own records
and declarations. The harness is developed with itself.

**Not yet.** In the source of this page, each item below is wrapped as a *straw dog* — naming the
condition that retires it and the ticket that will. That is how the harness marks anything
provisional, in its own rules as much as here; a script lists every one, so nothing provisional
passes for settled.

## Use it

    git clone https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness.git

From your project's root, have your coding agent read `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` in the
clone and follow it. It installs the harness, reports what arrived, and sets up your project's own
rules with you — its checks and its switches. What it runs is one script,

says why. Updating to a later version and checking the installed copy are in the same skill.
Python 3.12 or later, standard library only. MIT licensed.
```

# The harness meets a tree that already has a method

- **Status:** Planned (RFC authored 2026-09-21; the scripts' namespace precedes)
- **Type:** HITL
- **Plan:** [The harness meets a tree that already has a method RFC](../rfc/01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md)
  — the inventory as one look over the four places; the flow as instruction, with collisions
  and a process of the project's own at `/align`, and an anchor for mechanisms' meet-blocks
- **Depends on:** [01-0010.0130](./done/01-0010.0130-harness-installs-into-another-tree.md) (the
  install, its refusals, the stamp and the skill this slice extends);
  [01-0010.0145](./done/01-0010.0145-core-scripts-under-one-directory.md) (core's scripts under a
  directory of their own, so an install into a foreign `.agents/` cannot overwrite a project's)
- **Outcome:** An install into a tree that already has a method — this harness taken by hand, or a
  stranger's entry file, stub, skills and process — ends with that method's content carried into
  the local file or a claimed skill, aligned with the user where it collides with core, or left
  where it is, never lost; and the skill says each step.

## Parent

[Shared harness across projects](./01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md), whose
[existing-tree delivery](./01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md#existing-tree-delivery--2026-09-21)
holds the `/impact`. Carved from the install the day
[01-0010.0130](./done/01-0010.0130-harness-installs-into-another-tree.md) closed, at the user's
questions: is the instance expected to run the skill; does it say how to find local overrides in
an existing corpus; will it delete existing skills; can it say how to integrate them. The answers
were yes, no, no and no, and the three noes are this slice.

## What to build

Decided at the align of 2026-09-21 *(the user)*:

- **The refusal carries an inventory.** When `--install` meets the project's own entry file, a
  stub with content, a skill directory where a loader link goes, or a file at a path the
  manifest would write, it still writes nothing — but the refusal names everything it found, not
  the first thing in the way: each file with its size, each skill directory with its skill names,
  so the agent knows what it is integrating before it moves anything. A stranger harness is the
  same refusal with more in the inventory. **An `.agents/` of another convention is not, by
  itself, a refusal** *(the user, 2026-09-21, at `/plan`)*: the install integrates into it, and
  only a file standing where the manifest writes is a collision. So that core's scripts can never
  collide with a project's, they are namespaced under their own directory — a slice of its own,
  which this one depends on.
- **The flow is explicit in the skill**, for a tree with any existing method: run the install;
  read the inventory; for each finding, amend the instance where it is trivial — a fact or a
  convention becomes a local rule, a project skill moves under `.agents/skills/` with its claim
  line so the loader link reaches it and the shape check accepts it, the old entry file moves
  aside once every line of it has a home — and `/align` with the user where it is not: a rule
  that contradicts core's, which becomes an override naming it or a decision; **a skill that
  collides with one of core's, in either of two ways** *(the user, 2026-09-21)*: by name — the
  project's `plan` is not core's `plan` — or by responsibility — the project's `review` does what
  core's `verify` does; and **a process of the project's own**, which the flow meets step by
  step at `/align` for now, since the loop's granularity and ceremony are not yet switchable —
  the pacer's, [01-0020](./01-0020-pacer.md). Then run the install again, populate the local
  file, and check. Nothing of the project's is deleted by the script at any step, and the skill
  says so. The flow's section is an anchor: a mechanism that has said how it meets an existing
  method — the ticket mechanism first, for work tracked on a board or in another shape — installs
  its block there through its rules file, and the flow says so in one line.
- **The README is a front page**, not a second home for the flow: what this is in two sentences,
  the clone line, and *read `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` and follow it*. The flow has one
  owner.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An install into a tree holding its own entry file, a stub with content, a skill directory
      where a link goes, or a file at a path the manifest writes, writes nothing and reports
      every one of them it found, with the skill names under each directory; an install into a
      tree whose `.agents/` holds only files the manifest does not write proceeds and reports
      them as the project's own.
- [ ] The skill states the flow for an existing tree, step by step, including what is amended
      without asking, what goes to `/align` — a rule against core's, a skill colliding by name or
      by responsibility, a process of the project's own — and that the script deletes nothing of
      the project's; its section carries the line under which a mechanism's own meet-block lands.
- [ ] The README carries the clone line and a pointer to the skill and no step of the flow.
- [ ] Behavioural tests cover the inventory on each of the four findings, each alone and all at
      once, and an install into a foreign `.agents/` that collides on nothing.
- [ ] A real stranger tree — one of the user's estates with its own corpus — takes an install
      by the skill's flow, graded by the user in that tree.
- [ ] `/verify` has been run on this ticket against its ticket, RFC, and governing docs.

## Out of scope

Deleting or rewriting a project's own skills, which stays the agent's under the flow and never the
script's. The repository line in the skill —
[01-0010.0155](./done/01-0010.0155-a-tree-names-the-repository-its-core-comes-from.md), carved out at
`/plan`. What an update says about what moved —
[01-0010.0160](./01-0010.0160-harness-edge-changes-reach-an-update.md). Contribution back — the
spec's *Out of Scope*. Whether a host reads the loader link —
[01-0010.0120](./01-0010.0120-host-delivery-surfaces.md). The loop's switchability —
[01-0020](./01-0020-pacer.md).

## Parent scope addressed

The parent's promise that projects receive the method while preserving project-specific behavior,
taken for a project that already has some.

## How it works

Core reaches a tree from a fresh clone of its repository at a ref and never from a working tree,
so what a recipient holds is what a commit holds. The manifest is everything under the core
directory plus the entry file and the host stub; the project's local file is never in it, which
is what lets a redeploy overwrite core's content and nothing of the project's. What ships is
transformed before a byte is written: the origin's local blocks removed, every straw-dog wrapper
and every `TODO`'s ticket binding sheared with the content kept, the announce line stamped, and
the whole held to the leak rule the origin's check applies.

**The announce line is the revision.** A recipient's entry file reads
`Entry contract: <repository>@<ref>, <date>.`; every session there announces it, the check reads
it, and the shape check reads its `@` to know it stands in a recipient — where an unbound
`not yet` is upstream's gap and draws nothing. No record file: integrity is asked of the source,
by cloning the announced ref again and comparing. A change to the transformation therefore reads
as an edit in every recipient installed before it, until it updates. What the announced ref
shipped is read under the transformation alone, never held to today's shipping refusals: those
govern what may leave now, and a rule added after a ref shipped would otherwise strand every tree
that took it.

**The repository line is the source, as the announce line is the ref.** The harness skill carries
`Repository: <url>`, the only authored home of where core comes from: the script keeps no
constant and reads its default there, an install stamps a recipient's copy with the source the
run actually read — a URL verbatim, a path resolved absolute — and a fork edits the line once and
everything it installs names the fork. Both lines are the recipient's own facts living in core
files, so both are set aside when a copy is compared: a check or an update run from another
`--from` reads no edit in core. A stamped source is never a citation either, which the citation
reader settles for every reader of it, so a clone kept under a `docs/` directory does not make a
recipient fail its own shape check.

**Every refusal writes nothing**, and the loader links are the one step a person may finish by
hand: where the platform refuses to create a symlink, the run finishes everything else and ends
with the exact elevated command. Nothing is substituted for a link; a junction is refused by name.

**The gate is the check, and it takes seconds.** Arrival and any later day's question are one
function: the copy against the ref, the injector's check, the shape check — the target's own
scripts, run as subprocesses, so what is checked is what arrived. The loader links are reported
beside the verdict and never decide it: a link the platform refused is the person's one
remaining step, and its command is already in the report. The shipped suite is not run here —
it costs minutes, and an install is seconds — a recipient that wants it names it in its own
verification set *(the user, 2026-09-21)*.

It is **installed**; a tree without it holds no core at all. The repository's root `README.md`
is not a part: it never ships, and a recipient has its own.

## Moments

| moment | instructed by | kind, and why |
|---|---|---|
| installing a ref into an empty tree | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| updating a tree that has a copy | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| checking a copy against the ref it announces | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| making a loader link, or handing the person the command | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| reading a refusal and resuming | `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` | |
| populating the local file after the first install | `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` | |
| pointing a tree at another core, as a fork does | `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` | |
| knowing an update is available | — | unowned by design — a person asks for one; nothing polls the repository |
| verifying that a host reads the loader link | — | <straw-dog until="a host's delivery is observed rather than assumed" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0010.0120-host-delivery-surfaces.md">not yet</straw-dog> |
| writing a fresh tree's delivery status | `.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py` | |
| removing one mechanism from a tree | — | <straw-dog until="the parts tables say what goes and something says how" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md">not yet</straw-dog> |
| sending a change back to the repository | — | <straw-dog until="contribution back has a shape" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0010-dev-harness-shared-and-local.md">not yet</straw-dog> |

| part | where |
|---|---|
| instruction file | `.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md` |
| this doc | `.agents/mechanisms/harness/harness.md` |

- **The stamped announce line** — announced by the recipient's first reply; read by `--check` and

# The front page says what the harness is — implementation plan

**Authored:** 2026-09-26

Implements [01-0010.0167](../tickets/01-0010.0167-the-front-page-says-what-the-harness-is.md).

## Governing decisions

- **The manifest carries the license** — [architecture](../architecture.md), the install contract,
  and the [harness doc](../../.agents/mechanisms/harness/harness.md), *How it works*, both landed
  2026-09-26: one home at the source's root `LICENSE`, placed under the core directory as
  `.agents/LICENSE`; a ref without one ships none.
- **Core and instance** — [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#core-and-instance): the page points into core
  only. `docs/` appears in it nowhere but the straw dogs' bindings, which a release shears
  ([01-0010.0190](../tickets/01-0010.0190-core-is-published-as-a-release.md)).
- **Straw dogs** — [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md#straw-dogs): each *not yet* item is wrapped where
  it is written, its body standing alone.
- **The page's text** is the ticket's *The page, as the align settled it*, with its bindings table.

## What changes

### The license travels

`Source.files` reads the root license apart from the archive and places it at `.agents/LICENSE`
among the files it returns. Apart, because `git archive` refuses a pathspec that matches nothing —
`git archive 1475df1 -- .agents AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md LICENSE` exits 128 — and every ref before this
one has no root license: naming it in the archive would refuse every existing tree's update and
check, [rule failure 9](../rule-failures.md)'s class. Read as the commit's blob, so no line-ending
conversion touches it; absent, nothing is added.

Everything else follows from the existing machinery and needs no new flow:

- `shipped` passes it through verbatim — neither `.md` nor `.py`.
- An install writes it, and refuses when the target already holds a file there, as for any
  manifest path.
- An update replaces it, and a later ref that drops it deletes it, as what left the manifest.
- `--check`'s ref gate compares it like any core file, so an edited one fails the gate.
- `Shipment.earlier` over a pre-license ref reads none and refuses nothing.

The harness skill's *What a run does* names it beside the entry file and the host stub. The harness
doc's parts table gains no row: the license lives at two paths — the source's root and a
recipient's `.agents/` — which one row cannot name, and the shape check reads every row in every
tree; the prose under the table says so, as it does for the loader links.

### The page

The root `README.md` becomes the ticket's text. Its links, all into core: `AGENTS.md`,
`.agents/skills/`, `.agents/glossary.md`, the four format files
(`.agents/skills/ticket/TICKET-FORMAT.md`, `.agents/skills/align/ADR-FORMAT.md`,
`ARCH-FORMAT.md`, `GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md`), `.agents/mechanisms/ticket/ticket.rules.md`,
`.agents/skills/harness/SKILL.md`, and `LICENSE`. The eight *not yet* items are list items each
wrapped inline, `until` the named ticket's completion and bound per the ticket's table.

### The listing reaches the page

`/maintain`'s **T1** names `README.md` among what `straw_dogs.py` reads, and the queue's line on the
verification set says the same; otherwise *a script lists every one* is false of the page's own
examples.

## Impact

**Must change:** `Source.files` and its docstring; `test_harness.py`'s source seed, which gains a
root license so every two-tree case ships one; the harness skill's *What a run does*; the harness
doc's note under its parts table; the root README; `/maintain`'s T1; the queue's verification-set
line.

**Must verify:** `ATreeInstalledUnderEarlierRules` — an earlier ref without a license updates and
the update writes one; `AnUpdateAcrossTheScriptsMove`; every install assertion over `written` or the
manifest, which gains one path; the three gates in a real install from the pushed ref.

**May simplify:** nothing.

**Hidden edges:**

- **An update writes a new manifest path over whatever the recipient holds there.** An install

```markdown
# GoodWolf Harness

Coding agents are capable engineers who forget everything when the session ends — and a different
one arrives next time. The harness gives that workforce an institutional memory in the repository:
what was decided and why, what is unfinished, what was verified and against what. Each session
reconstructs where the project stands from those records, not from a chat that is gone.

The harness is yours to change. Your project's own rules — its test commands, whether the agent may
commit without asking — go in one local file that every install and update applies last; to change
a shipped rule, you override it there by name. You can add skills of your own: `/mechanism`, the
skill for declaring one, walks you through it, and the same checks then hold your skill as hold the
shipped ones. And when a rule was in place but the agent didn't follow it, the case is written down
and the rule reworded — a postmortem aimed at the instructions instead of the code.

## How it works

A session starts with `/recall`, which reads the project's records and finds where the work
stopped. `/align` settles with you whatever needs deciding, and the work picks up from there — one
step or several, through as many pieces of work as the session holds — until `/conclude` writes
down what the next session needs. A piece of work moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` →
`/verify` → `/maintain`: it becomes a ticket with checkable acceptance criteria, gets a written
plan, is built test-first where it can be, and is verified against its ticket, its plan and the
project's own checks. Whenever a step needs a decision, it goes back to `/align`. `/maintain` is a
separate step for drift: it checks that the repository's documents still agree with each other and
with the code, and repairs what doesn't.

Decisions live in the architecture, ADRs and glossary; open work lives in tickets; session records
are history, never the authority on what is still open. What each record looks like is in its
format file: tickets, ADRs, architecture, glossary.

Where a person has to say yes is a switch — commit, push, start the next piece of work, split work
into tickets — each `ask` or `auto`, and one more for whether a clear rule violation is fixed and
reported or shown to you first:

    commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report

The loop and its rules are in AGENTS.md, every skill under `.agents/skills/`, and the harness's
vocabulary in `.agents/glossary.md`.

## What holds it together

- **Two looks before a decision.** `/impact` looks inward: what a change touches in this project,
  and whether a mistake there would break one part or several. `/discover` looks outward: it hands
  the question to a separate agent that hasn't read the project, so you get an outside view of what
  the thing is and how things like it usually go wrong before settling on your own.
- **One home per rule.** A rule is written once, in its owner's rules file, and copied into every
  skill that reads it — in AGENTS.md you can see such a copy, `<installed by="ticket">`, whose
  source is `ticket.rules.md`. A copy that drifts from its source, or that nothing owns, fails the
  check.
- **Rules that fail get reworded.** When a rule was in place and the agent didn't follow it, the
  case is written down — which rules were in play, why this one didn't fire, how it is reworded —
  and the next time the situation comes up shows whether the rewording worked.
- **Every part of the method says what it is.** A skill that other work relies on is declared
  through `/mechanism`: its parts, the moments a person acts on it, what it produces and who reads
  that. A script checks the declaration is true.
- **The checks travel.** An install ends by running them inside your project, and your project can
  keep them in its own verification.

it to a later version, and checking that the installed copy is intact, with your project's own
rules applied last; one home per rule, with drift detection; checks on the harness's own records
and declarations. The harness is developed with itself.

condition that retires it and the ticket that will. That is how the harness marks anything
provisional, in its own rules as much as here; a script lists every one, so nothing provisional
passes for settled.

    git clone https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness.git

clone and follow it. It installs the harness, reports what arrived, and sets up your project's own
rules with you — its checks and its switches. What it runs is one script,
`python <clone>/.agents/scripts/gw/harness.py . --install`, which writes nothing if it refuses and
says why. Updating to a later version and checking the installed copy are in the same skill.
Python 3.12 or later, standard library only. MIT licensed.
```

The plan for the front page is written, in [its RFC](docs/rfc/01-0010.0167-the-front-page-says-what-the-harness-is.md). Nothing is committed.

**The one real design catch:** installs can't copy the license by simply adding `LICENSE` to what gets archived. `git archive` fails outright on a path that doesn't exist in a version (I ran it: exit 128), and no existing version has a root LICENSE. So that would have broken every existing tree's update and check again, the same failure as the one we fixed earlier. The plan reads the license separately and skips it when a version doesn't have one. Everything else (install, update, check, deletion) handles the file with no new code.

**What landed alongside the plan:**
- **The license decision is in the durable docs.** [architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) and [harness.md](.agents/mechanisms/harness/harness.md) now say: one home at the root, installed as `.agents/LICENSE`, and a version without one ships none.
- **The agreed README text now lives in the RFC.** The ticket's format check rejected it inside the ticket, because the checker counted the page's `##` headings even inside a code block. That's a small checker defect worth fixing another time. The ticket keeps the decisions and the bindings table.

**Four stages:**
1. Tests first, then the code change:
   - an install places `.agents/LICENSE`, byte-identical;
   - the project's own root `LICENSE` is left alone;
   - an update carries a changed license;
   - `--check` catches an edited one;
   - an old version with no license still installs and updates;
   - an install refuses when the project already holds `.agents/LICENSE`.
2. Docs: the harness skill's line, and the harness doc's note on why the license isn't a row in its parts table (it lives at two different paths).
3. The README, and the straw-dog listing extended to it, so all eight "not yet" items are listed.
4. Live check: how GitHub actually renders the straw-dog tags, and a real install from the pushed version.

**Hidden risk, not this slice's to fix:** an update writes a newly shipped file over whatever a project already has at that path. An install checks for that; an update doesn't. Neither of your real projects has an `.agents/LICENSE`, and the gap belongs to .0150's collision work.
